organic:oc-vqku6.w: It is a meso compound. Both chlorine-bearing carbons are stereocenters, but a mirror plane through C2 and C5 maps one onto the other, so the molecule is achiral and does not rotate light.
s: C1 and C3 each hold Cl, H and two different ring paths: **stereocenters**.
In the cis isomer both Cl point to the same face.
A **mirror plane** runs through C2 and C5.
Stereocenters plus an internal mirror plane: **meso**, optically inactive.
t: That describes trans-1,3-dichlorocyclohexane, which has no mirror plane. The cis isomer does.
It is a constitutional isomer of the 1,4 compound, but the mirror plane makes it optically inactive.
Its mirror image can be laid exactly on top of it, which is what achiral means.
C1 and C3 are stereocenters: each carries Cl, H and two ring paths that differ. The molecule is achiral for another reason.
c: Is trans-1,3-dichlorocyclohexane chiral?
Yes. It has no mirror plane and exists as a pair of enantiomers.

organic:oc-8gdlsf.w: The major product is isopropylbenzene (cumene). The propyl group rearranges by a hydride shift from a primary to a secondary cation before the ring attacks.
s: AlCl3 pulls chloride off: a **primary** propyl cation starts to form.
A neighboring H shifts with its pair: the **secondary** isopropyl cation.
Benzene attacks that cation.
Loss of H+ restores the ring: **isopropylbenzene**.
t: Ethylbenzene has only two carbons on the ring. Three carbons went in and none are lost.
Propylbenzene is the unrearranged product. The primary cation shifts a hydride first, so this is the minor product.
A tert-butyl group has four carbons. The alkyl halide supplies only three.
An isobutyl group has four carbons, one more than 1-chloropropane provides.
c: How would you make propylbenzene without rearrangement?
Friedel-Crafts acylation with propanoyl chloride, then reduce the ketone. Acylium ions do not rearrange.

organic:oc-1v0wmr4.w: The major product is 3,3-dimethyl-1-butene. E2 happens in one step with no cation, so nothing rearranges, and the only neighboring hydrogens are on the CH3 group.
s: Strong base plus heat on a secondary halide: **E2**.
E2 is one step: **no cation**, no shifts.
Find beta hydrogens: the CH3 has three, the tert-butyl carbon has **none**.
Remove a CH3 hydrogen: the terminal alkene, 3,3-dimethyl-1-butene.
t: 2,3-Dimethyl-1-butene has a rearranged skeleton. A methyl shift needs a cation, and E2 never makes one.
2,3-Dimethyl-2-butene is the rearranged, most substituted alkene. That is the E1 answer, not the E2 answer.
The ethyl ether is the SN2 product. This carbon sits next to a tert-butyl group, so with hot strong base elimination wins.
An alcohol would need water or hydroxide as the nucleophile. The base here is ethoxide, and it eliminates.
c: Under E1 conditions (warm ethanol, no strong base), which alkene is major?
2,3-Dimethyl-2-butene, after a methyl shift to the tertiary cation.

organic:oc-1mnmhwn.w: A roughly equal mixture of 2-pentanone and 3-pentanone forms. Both alkyne carbons carry one alkyl group, so water has no strong preference, and each enol tautomerizes to a ketone.
s: Hg(II) and acid add **water** across the triple bond.
Each alkyne carbon has one alkyl group: **no Markovnikov preference**.
OH on C2 gives an enol that becomes **2-pentanone**.
OH on C3 gives **3-pentanone**.
Result: a mixture of both ketones.
t: Hydration adds water; it does not break the carbon chain. Cleavage to acids needs ozone or hot KMnO4.
An aldehyde needs the oxygen on a chain-end carbon. Both alkyne carbons here are internal, so only ketones form.
Internal alkynes do react with Hg(II) and aqueous acid. They just give ketone mixtures when unsymmetrical.
Methyl and ethyl stabilize a positive charge about equally, so C2 is not strongly preferred over C3.
c: What does the same reagent give with 1-pentyne?
2-Pentanone only. A terminal alkyne has a clear Markovnikov carbon.

organic:oc-1boz2p7.w: Only the beta-keto acid loses CO2 easily on heating. Its ketone oxygen sits where it can accept the acid proton through a six-membered ring transition state; in the gamma-keto acid the ketone is one carbon too far.
s: Easy decarboxylation needs a C=O **beta** to the COOH.
The ketone oxygen takes the acid H through a **six-membered** ring.
CO2 leaves and an **enol** forms, then becomes a ketone.
In the gamma-keto acid that ring would be seven-membered: no easy path.
t: More distance does not help. The proton transfer needs the six-membered arrangement only a beta carbonyl gives.
Having a ketone is not enough. Its position relative to the COOH decides it.
A beta ketone does assist: it accepts the proton as CO2 leaves. That is why beta-keto acids decarboxylate on warming.
A lactone comes from a hydroxy acid, not a keto acid, and making one does not release CO2.
c: What forms when 3-oxo-3-phenylpropanoic acid is heated?
Acetophenone and CO2.

organic:oc-8neusk.w: The major product is 2-bromo-2,3-dimethylbutane. Protonation gives a secondary cation next to a quaternary carbon, a methyl group shifts over, and bromide adds to the new tertiary cation.
s: H+ adds to the **end carbon**: a secondary cation at C2.
C3 is quaternary: it has **no H** to shift, only methyls.
A **methyl shifts** with its pair from C3 to C2.
The charge is now **tertiary** at C3.
Bromide adds there: 2-bromo-2,3-dimethylbutane.
t: This has the rearranged skeleton but puts Br on a primary carbon. Bromide adds where the positive charge is, on the tertiary carbon.
Bromine on the end carbon is the anti-Markovnikov product, which needs peroxides.
This carbon skeleton does not come from any shift of this cation, and its Br is on a primary carbon.
This is the unrearranged secondary bromide. The methyl shift to a tertiary cation is faster than capture by bromide.
c: Why is it a methyl shift here and not a hydride shift?
The neighboring carbon is quaternary. It has no hydrogen to give, only methyl groups.

organic:oc-yraq7h.w: Anilinium is the strongest acid (pKa about 4.6, against about 5.2 for pyridinium and 10.6 for methylammonium). The weakest base has the strongest conjugate acid, and aniline is the weakest base because its lone pair is spread into the ring.
s: Strongest acid means **weakest conjugate base**.
Aniline's lone pair is **delocalized** into the ring: weak base.
Pyridine's lone pair is in an sp2 orbital: also weak, slightly less so.
Methylamine's lone pair is localized and alkyl-boosted: strongest base.
Acid order: anilinium, then pyridinium, then methylammonium.
t: Losing an N-H proton is the same step, but the bases left behind differ a great deal in stability, so the pKa values differ.
Methylammonium has a pKa near 10.6, the highest of the three. It is the weakest acid, not the strongest.
Pyridine is a weaker base than methylamine, not a stronger one. Pyridinium is close to anilinium but slightly less acidic.
Alkyl donation makes methylamine the strongest base of the three, which makes its cation the weakest acid.
c: Which is the stronger base, pyridine or methylamine?
Methylamine. Its lone pair sits in an sp3 orbital, held less tightly than pyridine's sp2 pair.

organic:oc-p5414p.w: The product is the trans epoxide, trans-3,4-epoxyhexane. mCPBA delivers the oxygen to one face in a single step, so the two ethyl groups keep the trans relationship they had in the alkene.
s: mCPBA adds one **oxygen** across the C=C: an epoxide.
Both C-O bonds form at once on the **same face**.
Nothing rotates, so the alkene geometry is **kept**.
E alkene in, **trans** epoxide out (ethyls on opposite faces).
t: This is the cis epoxide, with both ethyl groups on the same face. It is what (Z)-3-hexene gives.
This shows an epoxide with no stereochemistry. The reaction is stereospecific, so the answer has to show trans.
A diol is one step further. Epoxidation stops at the epoxide unless aqueous acid opens the ring.
A diol needs OsO4 or acid opening of the epoxide. mCPBA alone stops at the epoxide.
c: What does (Z)-3-hexene give with mCPBA?
The cis epoxide, which is a meso compound.

organic:oc-csbizj.w: The product is ethyl 2-oxocyclohexanecarboxylate, a six-membered ring. The enolate next to one ester attacks the other ester carbonyl, ethoxide leaves, and a seven-carbon diester closes to a six-membered beta-ketoester.
s: Ethoxide removes an **alpha H** next to one ester.
That carbon (C2) attacks the far ester carbonyl (**C7**).
Ring atoms are C2 through C7: **six-membered**.
Ethoxide leaves: a ketone next to the ester carbon, a **beta-ketoester**.
t: The open-chain beta-keto diester comes from two molecules reacting. Closing a six-membered ring within one molecule is faster.
A five-membered ring is what diethyl adipate, one carbon shorter, would give.
A seven-membered ring would need an eight-carbon diester. Ring size is chain length minus one.
A Claisen-type condensation ends in a ketone because ethoxide leaves. A hydroxy ester would be an aldol-type product.
c: What ring size does diethyl adipate (six carbons) give in a Dieckmann condensation?
Five.

organic:oc-1olhj21.w: Add aqueous HCl. Aniline is a base, so acid protonates it to anilinium chloride, a salt that moves into the water layer while the hydrocarbon stays in the ether.
s: Aniline is a **base** (an amine).
Acid protonates it: **anilinium chloride**.
Charged salts dissolve in **water**, not ether.
The neutral hydrocarbon stays in the ether layer.
t: Bicarbonate is a weak base. It pulls carboxylic acids into water but does nothing to an amine.
Brine only helps remove water from the organic layer. It transfers no proton.
MgSO4 is a solid drying agent. It removes traces of water and ionizes nothing.
NaOH is a base, so the amine stays neutral and stays in the ether. NaOH extracts acids such as phenols.
c: How do you recover aniline from the aqueous HCl layer?
Add NaOH to deprotonate the anilinium, then extract the neutral amine back into ether.

organic:oc-163l4so.w: The aldehyde is reduced first. Its carbonyl carbon has one alkyl group instead of two, so it is more electron-poor and less crowded, and one equivalent of NaBH4 goes there.
s: Hydride attacks the **carbonyl carbon**.
The aldehyde carbon holds one alkyl group and an H.
Less donation: **more electrophilic**. Less bulk: **easier to reach**.
With one equivalent, the aldehyde reacts and the ketone is left.
t: Alkyl groups donate electrons, so two of them make the ketone carbon less electrophilic, not more.
The right carbonyl for the wrong reason. The aldehyde is the less hindered one.
NaBH4 reduces aldehydes and ketones. Esters are the group it normally leaves alone.
NaBH4 is selective when it is limited: aldehydes react faster than ketones.
c: What is the product here?
5-Hydroxypentan-2-one: the aldehyde becomes a primary alcohol and the ketone is untouched.

organic:oc-9wwa4n.w: Two ketones. Each alkene carbon of 1,2-dimethylcyclopentene carries a methyl and a ring carbon and no hydrogen, so cleaving the C=C leaves a ketone at both ends: heptane-2,6-dione.
s: Ozonolysis cuts the C=C and puts **C=O** on each carbon.
Check each alkene carbon for an **H**.
Both carry a methyl and a ring carbon: **no H**.
No H means a **ketone** on each side.
The ring opens to one chain: a diketone.
t: An aldehyde needs a hydrogen on the alkene carbon. Neither alkene carbon has one.
Acids come from alkene carbons with an H under oxidizing workup. Here there is no H, and zinc workup is reducing.
A carboxylic acid would need a vinylic H and an oxidizing workup. Neither applies.
That would fit 1-methylcyclopentene, where one alkene carbon has an H. Here both are fully substituted.
c: What does 1-methylcyclopentene give with O3, then Zn?
A keto-aldehyde, 5-oxohexanal: one alkene carbon has an H and one does not.

organic:oc-1oitbuh.w: Cyclohexane. H2 with palladium adds one hydrogen to each alkene carbon and nothing else.
s: The reagent is **H2** on a metal surface.
It adds one H to each **alkene carbon**.
No oxygen or halogen is present to add.
Cyclohexene becomes **cyclohexane**.
t: Cyclohexanol would need water added across the double bond. Hydrogenation adds only hydrogen.
Benzene has more double bonds, not fewer. That is the reverse direction.
A dibromide needs Br2, which is not in the flask.
Cyclohexanone needs an oxygen source and an oxidation. This is a reduction.
c: Do the two hydrogens add to the same face or opposite faces?
The same face (syn), because both come from the metal surface.

organic:oc-1rhxjv.w: The product is cis-3-octene. NaNH2 makes the acetylide, bromoethane adds two carbons to give 3-octyne, and Lindlar's catalyst adds one H2 to the same face to give the cis alkene.
s: NaNH2 removes the terminal alkyne H: an **acetylide**.
The acetylide attacks bromoethane (SN2): **3-octyne**.
Lindlar adds **one H2**, both H on the same face.
Result: the **cis** alkene, cis-3-octene.
t: cis-2-Octene has the double bond one carbon off. Adding an ethyl group puts the alkyne, then the alkene, at C3.
Octane is full reduction. That takes H2 with ordinary Pd or Pt, not the poisoned Lindlar catalyst.
3-Octyne is the product after step 2. Step 3 still reduces it.
The trans alkene comes from sodium in liquid ammonia. Lindlar gives cis.
c: Which reagent turns 3-octyne into trans-3-octene?
Sodium (or lithium) in liquid ammonia.

organic:oc-y8rsnv.w: The product is (S)-2-phenylpropan-1-amine. LiAlH4 turns the amide C=O into CH2 and keeps the nitrogen, and no bond to the stereocenter is touched, so its configuration stays the same.
s: LiAlH4 reduces an amide to an **amine**.
The **C=O becomes CH2**; nitrogen stays.
The stereocenter is the next carbon over: no bond to it breaks.
Its arrangement is **retained**: (S)-2-phenylpropan-1-amine.
t: This is the mirror-image configuration. The reaction happens at the carbonyl carbon, so the stereocenter cannot invert.
This adds a methyl group to the ring. LiAlH4 delivers hydrogen only.
The aldehyde has lost the nitrogen. LiAlH4 takes an amide all the way to the amine.
The alcohol is what an ester or acid gives. An amide keeps its nitrogen and loses its oxygen.
c: What does LiAlH4 give with an ester, RCOOR'?
Two alcohols: RCH2OH and R'OH.
